lesson.menu_title: Money, Power and Success — What Gets Said at the Table and What Does Not
lesson.menu_desc: The economy in English without the numbers, and the three modals that carry an opinion -- 36 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 12 -- Money, Power and Success
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Braulio Zemel | Lesson 12 -- Money, Power and Success
lesson.grammar_point: would rather, had better and may as well

listenings.text: Right, three things on the economy and then I will let you eat. First, the number everybody quoted last week was a valuation, not a price, and a valuation is somebody's opinion with a decimal point in it. Second, when people say the market is liquid they mean you can sell without moving the price, and that is a very different question from whether the thing is worth anything. And third, on the bubble question, which somebody always asks me. I would rather not use the word bubble at all. Every bubble is obvious afterwards and invisible while you are inside it, and anybody who tells you they can see one from the inside is selling something. What I would say is this. If you cannot explain where the yield is coming from, you had better assume you are the yield.

Here is something nobody explains to people who move between countries, and it costs them at every dinner. In English, and particularly in American English, you can talk about money for an hour without ever mentioning your own. The subject is the economy, the market, the currency, the policy. It is never how much you have, what you paid for the house, or what you earned before you stopped. Asking any of those things is not rude in the way that shouting is rude. It is rude in a quieter way. It puts the other person in a position where every possible answer is uncomfortable. The rule is simple once you see it. Talk about money in the third person. Numbers about the world are conversation. Numbers about the people at the table are an intrusion, and the only person who may safely bring up your finances is you.

extra_audio.text: Margaret asks Braulio whether people in Brazil talk about money as openly as they do about politics. He answers that they talk about the economy all the time, and about their own salaries almost never. Margaret says that in her experience the same rule holds in most places, and that the exception is people who have just made money. Braulio asks her how she handles the question when somebody asks her directly what she used to earn. She tells him that she would rather answer with a number about the market than with a number about herself.

reading.rtitle: Talking About Money Without Talking About Yours
paras: There is a conversation about money that runs at almost every international dinner table, and it has a rule that nobody states out loud. You can talk about money for an hour, with real numbers and real disagreement, as long as none of the numbers belongs to anybody in the room.

The subjects that are open are the economy, the currency, the market, the policy and the price of a house in the abstract. The subjects that are closed are what you earn, what you earned, what you paid, and what you are worth. Asking is not rude the way that shouting is rude. It is rude in a quieter way, because it hands the other person a question where every possible answer is uncomfortable: the true one sounds like a boast or a complaint, and the evasive one sounds like a lie.

This catches people out in both directions. Somebody who comes from a culture where salaries are discussed freely reads the English silence as coldness. Somebody who comes from the opposite direction hears an hour of confident talk about valuations and yields and assumes the people at the table are all wealthy, when in fact they are simply talking in the third person, which costs nothing and reveals nothing.

The practical consequence is that you need two vocabularies and only one of them is technical. The technical one is easy and you already half have it from reading. The other one is a set of exits: what to say when the question does arrive, how to answer without answering, and how to move the conversation back out to the world. Those exits are worth more at a dinner than any amount of economics.
reading.source: Article -- The Long View, a newsletter about work and what comes after it
